hook: A farm sorts its eggs by weight: small, large, jumbo. It cannot weigh every possible egg in advance, but egg weights follow a smooth, bell-shaped pattern. With a curve, a mean of 58 grams and a standard deviation of 4 grams, the farm can predict what share of tomorrow's eggs will be jumbo.

prereq.q: A value is 6 above the mean and the standard deviation is 4. What is its z-score?
Which describes a distribution with a single peak and matching tails on both sides?
prereq.why: Matching tails on both sides mean symmetric.

figure.caption: Egg weights modeled by a normal curve with mean 58 g and SD 4 g: about 68%, 95% and 99.7% within 1, 2 and 3 SDs.

chain.cause: A distribution is roughly symmetric and bell-shaped
chain.effect: a normal curve $N(\mu, \sigma)$ can model it, and areas under the curve are probabilities

chain.cause: Every normal curve has the same shape in standard-deviation units
chain.effect: about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 SDs (the empirical rule)
any normal question becomes one about the standard normal $N(0, 1)$, answered by Table A or technology
inverse normal gives the z, then $x = \mu + z\sigma$ gives the boundary

ideas: A density curve is on or above the axis with total area 1; the area over an interval is the probability of that interval.
A normal distribution $N(\mu, \sigma)$ is symmetric and bell-shaped, centered at $\mu$ with spread $\sigma$. The standard normal is $N(0, 1)$.
The empirical rule: about 68%, 95% and 99.7% within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean.
Show work: name the distribution and parameters, the boundary and the direction, for example "$N(58, 4)$, $P(W > 66)$", with a sketch.
Forward: $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$, then the area. Backward: the area, then z, then $x = \mu + z\sigma$.

misconception.wrong: A normal model works for any data set once you know its mean and standard deviation.
misconception.right: A normal model fits only roughly symmetric, mound-shaped data. For strongly skewed data, normal areas give the wrong percents.

summary: A density curve models a distribution with areas as probabilities. Normal distributions $N(\mu, \sigma)$ are symmetric and bell-shaped, with about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values within 1, 2 and 3 SDs. Standardize with $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$ to find areas, or work back from an area to a boundary with $x = \mu + z\sigma$. Always name the distribution, parameters, boundary and direction.
